fields.Front: What are the core functional requirements to clarify for a Food Delivery System OOD interview?
fields.Back: 1) Customer browses a restaurant's menu and places an order. 2) Restaurant confirms/prepares the order. 3) A driver is assigned and delivers it. 4) The order's status is tracked end-to-end. 5) Payment is processed and can be refunded on cancellation/failure.

fields.Front: What should you explicitly mark out of scope when designing a Food Delivery System in an interview?
fields.Back: Real-time GPS routing/map algorithms, payment-gateway integration internals, and surge/dynamic pricing math — treat driver assignment and pricing as pluggable strategies rather than implementing the algorithms.

fields.Front: What is the responsibility of the Order class?
fields.Back: Holds the customer, restaurant, list of ordered MenuItems with quantities, total price, and its own OrderState; exposes advance() and cancel() but delegates the actual transition rules to its current state object.

fields.Front: What is the responsibility of the DispatchService class?
fields.Back: Maintains the pool of available drivers and, using a pluggable assignment strategy, matches an order that has entered preparation to a driver, then hands off tracking of the delivery leg.

fields.Front: What is the responsibility of the Restaurant class?
fields.Back: Holds identity/location data and its current MenuItem catalog (with availability toggles), and can accept or reject an incoming Order based on capacity/hours.

Aggregation through a line-item wrapper: Order holds a list of OrderLineItem (menuItem reference + quantity + any customizations), not raw MenuItems, so removing an item from the restaurant's menu later doesn't corrupt past orders.

Aggregation: DispatchService tracks a pool of currently-available Drivers (drivers exist independently of dispatch, e.g. they can be off-shift); it removes a driver from the pool on assignment and returns them after delivery completes.

fields.Front: Which design pattern fits the order lifecycle, and why?
fields.Back: State. Each status (Placed, Confirmed, Preparing, OutForDelivery, Delivered, Cancelled) is a state object that knows which transitions are legal from it; Order.advance() delegates to state.next(order), keeping transition rules out of a big switch statement and making illegal transitions (e.g. Delivered → Preparing) a compile-time-obvious non-option.

fields.Front: Which design pattern fits driver assignment, and why?
fields.Back: Strategy. A DriverAssignmentStrategy interface (e.g. NearestDriverStrategy, LoadBalancedStrategy) lets DispatchService swap the assignment algorithm — nearest driver at normal times, load-balanced during surge — without changing dispatch's calling code.

fields.Front: What does Order.advance() do, and why does Order not implement the transition logic itself?
fields.Back: It delegates to state.next(this), returning the new state to assign as this.state. Keeping the logic in state classes (not in Order) means adding a new status is a new class, and each state can encapsulate side effects specific to that transition (e.g. PreparingState.next() calls DispatchService.requestDriver()).

fields.Front: What is the shape of DispatchService's core API?
fields.Back: requestDriver(Order order) — delegates to the current DriverAssignmentStrategy and returns/assigns a Driver, raising a domain error if none is available — plus setStrategy(DriverAssignmentStrategy) to swap algorithms at runtime.

fields.Front: Edge case: an assigned driver cancels mid-delivery, after pickup. How should the design handle this?
fields.Back: The order stays in OUT_FOR_DELIVERY (not reverted to an earlier state); DispatchService is invoked again to find a replacement driver for the same order, and the customer is notified of the delay — the order's state machine doesn't need a new state, just a driver re-assignment at the dispatch layer.

fields.Front: Edge case: a restaurant can't fulfill an order after it was placed (e.g. out of an ingredient). How should this be modeled?
fields.Back: The restaurant transitions the order directly to CANCELLED from PLACED/CONFIRMED (a valid transition only from early states, enforced by the state classes), which triggers an automatic refund and a customer notification.

fields.Front: Edge case: no drivers are available in DispatchService's pool during a peak-hour rush. What should happen?
fields.Back: requestDriver() should not throw and drop the order; instead the order is queued for retry (exponential backoff or event-driven re-trigger when a driver becomes free), and the assignment strategy can itself be swapped to one that widens the search radius during surge.

fields.Front: (Java) Implement the OrderState interface and a PreparingState concrete implementation.
fields.Back:
public interface OrderState {
    OrderStatus getStatus();
    OrderState next(Order order);
}

public class PreparingState implements OrderState {
    @Override
    public OrderStatus getStatus() { return OrderStatus.PREPARING; }

    @Override
    public OrderState next(Order order) {
        DispatchService.getInstance().requestDriver(order);
        return new OutForDeliveryState();
    }
}

class DriverAssignmentStrategy:
    def assign(self, order, available_drivers):
        raise NotImplementedError


class NearestDriverStrategy(DriverAssignmentStrategy):
    def assign(self, order, available_drivers):
        restaurant_loc = order.restaurant.location
        return min(
            available_drivers,
            key=lambda d: distance(d.current_location, restaurant_loc),
            default=None,
        )

fields.Front: (Java) Implement Order.advance() and Order.cancel() using the State pattern.
fields.Back:
public class Order {
    private OrderState state;
    private final List<OrderLineItem> items;

    public void advance() {
        this.state = state.next(this);
    }

    public OrderStatus getStatus() {
        return state.getStatus();
    }

    public void cancel() {
        if (state.getStatus() == OrderStatus.DELIVERED) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot cancel a delivered order");
        }
        this.state = new CancelledState();
    }
}

fields.Front: (Python) Implement DispatchService.request_driver() with a swappable strategy and a no-drivers error.
fields.Back:
class DispatchService:
    def __init__(self, strategy):
        self.strategy = strategy
        self.available_drivers = []

    def set_strategy(self, strategy):
        self.strategy = strategy

    def request_driver(self, order):
        driver = self.strategy.assign(order, self.available_drivers)
        if driver is None:
            raise NoDriversAvailableError(order.id)
        driver.assign_order(order)
        self.available_drivers.remove(driver)
        return driver

fields.Text: The core classes in a Food Delivery System design are {{c1::Order}}, {{c2::Restaurant}} (with a menu), {{c3::MenuItem}}, {{c4::Driver}}, and {{c5::DispatchService}} (assigns drivers to orders).
The OrderStatus enum for order lifecycle is {{c1::PLACED}}, {{c2::CONFIRMED}}, {{c3::PREPARING}}, {{c4::OUT_FOR_DELIVERY}}, {{c5::DELIVERED}}, and {{c6::CANCELLED}}.
